prompt: Hypothetical. Win rate 30 percent, average win 3R, average loss 1R. What is the expectancy in R per trade?
solution: Win part = 0.30 x 3 = 0.90R. Loss rate = 0.70. Loss part = 0.70 x 1 = 0.70R. Expectancy = 0.90R - 0.70R = 0.20R per trade.

prompt: Which statement is the best hypothesis for an edge?

options.text: This method will make money next year.
If condition X occurs, the average trade result over 50 trades will be positive. The test uses data not used to design the rule.
I will trade when I feel confident about the market.
Price always returns after a fall, so buying after a fall works.

explanations.a: This is a promise about the future, with no condition and no test. A hypothesis must be something a test could prove wrong.
explanations.c: Confidence is a feeling. It cannot be tested, so it is not a rule.
explanations.d: This is a belief with no clear condition and no test. It also says the result always happens, which no test can confirm.

prompt: Hypothetical. A rule won 8 of its last 10 trades. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The rule has an edge, because 8 wins out of 10 is strong.
The result may be luck. Ten trades are too few to show an edge.
The rule has positive expectancy, because the win rate is high.
The rule has an edge only if costs are zero.

explanations.a: A high win rate on a small sample can come from luck. Ten trades cannot separate skill from luck.
explanations.c: A win rate alone does not give expectancy. The size of the wins and losses matters too.
explanations.d: Costs reduce expectancy, but this option does not explain why the sample is too small to show an edge.

prompt: Spot the mistake: "I designed the rule on last year's charts. It looked strong on those same charts, so the rule has an edge." Which part is wrong?

options.text: Testing on the same charts used to design the rule

explanations.a: Designing a rule on past data is normal. The error is in the testing step that follows.
explanations.c: The word strong describes the result. The error is that the result was not tested on fresh data.
explanations.d: The statement is not correct. A rule tested on the data used to build it always looks better than it is.

prompt: Hypothetical. Win rate 40 percent, average win 2R, average loss 1R, R = Rs 500. Assumed cost Rs 50 per trade. What is the expectancy after costs, in rupees per trade?
solution: Expectancy = 0.40 x 2R - 0.60 x 1R = 0.80R - 0.60R = 0.20R. In rupees: 0.20 x Rs 500 = Rs 100. After the Rs 50 cost: Rs 100 - Rs 50 = Rs 50 per trade.

prompt: Which statement about costs is correct?

options.text: Costs matter only for large accounts.
Costs reduce expectancy at any account size.
Costs are already included in the win rate.
Costs do not matter when the win rate is high.

explanations.a: Costs are a fixed amount on each trade. They take a share of each trade's result at any account size.
explanations.c: The win rate counts winning trades. It does not include the cost of each trade.
explanations.d: A high win rate does not remove costs. Costs still come out of every trade's result.
